title: Forearm swelling — next investigation
fairness: Ultrasonography is a defensible single best initial investigation among these choices. Skin mobility, direct-pressure tenderness and painless passive movement now support superficial localization; the explanation appropriately leaves the contents unconfirmed. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The localization observations are legitimate clinical evidence, not a wording-only giveaway. However, the competing MRI and radiography options have little positive support in this presentation. There is no actual motion-related complaint in the candidate to make the deeper-structure alternative particularly tempting.

Deleting the earlier redness and its treatment response still leaves essentially the same superficial-lump ultrasound question. The purported response-discrepancy step does not change the scored investigation. This is a useful, high-yield recognition/application rule but currently easy for the intended residents.
The named age/sex presentation and complete task stand alone. This is a single-node case with no preceding feedback or later result needed to answer it.
suggestions: Keep the repaired localization findings and conditional explanation. Introduce a supported, genuinely competing clinical consideration that changes the next investigation, then make both the interval course and examination necessary to resolve it. Do not manufacture difficulty by removing the localization needed for fairness.
If the intended objective remains uncomplicated superficial ultrasound selection, seek explicit acceptance as a basic item instead of claiming two consequential steps.

Report scope: nine current revised v2 decision nodes reviewed using candidate presentation, current update, task, options and explanation. No separate exhibits are supplied. The two pass-preserved v1 questions are noted as unchanged visible-content records and are not re-rated. Five historical kept records, 34 proposed retirement records, 15 parked v1 candidates, seven earlier withheld candidates and the withheld teaching point are noted, not reviewed as active questions. Archived versions and author self-assessments do not establish these verdicts.

Report-wide limits: this is an offline editorial review, not fresh source verification or Melissa Rowland's clinical sign-off. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified examination frequencies. Clinical drafts remain needs_clinician_review. Runtime wait rendering and execution are outside this candidate-text review.

title: Recurrent back swelling — radiolucent foreign-body assessment
fairness: The candidate supports targeted ultrasonography as the best next investigation: recurrence after drainage raises a residual local-source problem; the penetrating material and adequate negative radiographs must then be interpreted before choosing a superficial localization method. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The negative radiograph does not exclude the relevant material. Correct-site coverage is necessary to distinguish repeating an inadequately targeted study from changing modalities. CT remains a real anatomical alternative, but the superficial focus supports ultrasound first in the described situation.

The prior drainage note is evidence about an unresolved source, not the name of the keyed test. No key-only word match, conspicuous label-length advantage, convergence or rhetorical absolute identifies ultrasound without clinical knowledge.

The repeat-radiography distractor is weaker for a resident who knows the material limitation, so this is moderate rather than hard. Retained foreign material in recurrent local infection is a useful, commonly taught surgical concept.
The case is self-contained: the prior procedure and imaging results are supplied directly, without requiring an earlier question or explanation.

title: Persistent toe ulcer — advanced imaging

cues.phrase: The foot team needs to assess the underlying marrow and adjacent soft tissues before planning further treatment.
cues.why: This supplies the anatomical planning conclusion the resident should derive from the persistent tract and fullness. It is a pre-answer interpretation cue, rather than a purely lexical way for a medically uninformed reader to select MRI. Together with the advanced-imaging lead-in, it reduces the task to recalling the preferred modality.

fairness: MRI is a defensible preferred next advanced examination for the stated unresolved diabetic-foot bone and soft-tissue question. The offered nuclear studies are legitimate alternatives; their existence does not by itself make the best-answer task invalid. No confident clinical error identified.

The explanation's guideline-preference claim is not independently source-verified in this offline review. The feedback should continue to distinguish a preferred first examination from a claim that the alternatives cannot evaluate infection.

Initial diagnostic uncertainty and persisting local findings are clinically meaningful, but the final presentation sentence and lead-in have already selected the decision stage and intended assessment. The remaining discrimination is mostly a familiar guideline-recall choice, not two consequential inferences.

The current standalone presentation contains the relevant prior findings and needs no missing earlier answer. Diabetic-foot osteomyelitis workup is high-yield; obscurity of alternative test names should not be mistaken for clinical reasoning difficulty.
suggestions: Remove the authored marrow-and-soft-tissue planning conclusion while preserving the raw probing, radiographic and interval findings. Ask a neutral, complete next-investigation task.

Rebuild the competition around an actual unresolved decision established by those findings, so interpreting the initial workup changes the next step. Deleting the final sentence alone will not necessarily make a conventional MRI-recall item moderate or hard.

If retaining MRI versus nuclear alternatives, have clinical sign-off confirm their ranking for the exact case and keep the explanation conditional on that context. Do not invent a contraindication, availability restriction or diagnostic threshold to force the key.

title: Operative infection review — debridement extent

cues.phrase: retained tissue would be reassessed at the planned operation
cues.why: The update announces tissue retention and reassessment before the choice. It directly rehearses the option component 'retain perfused skin for reassessment', removing much of the skin-management decision.

cues.phrase: No additional nonviable skin or muscle was identified in the exposed field
cues.why: This interpretive conclusion, combined with already supplied bleeding and contraction observations, makes excision of the overlying skin sound gratuitous even to a reader relying on ordinary meanings of viable and nonviable. Necessary viability evidence should remain, but this wording supplies rather than tests its interpretation.

Against 'Resect fascia within the redness' and an update explicitly saying the abnormal fascia continues beyond redness, the complete-removal label has a strong common-sense advantage. The balanced four-option matrix avoids majority convergence but does not remove this completeness cue.

fairness: The candidate supplies enough viability and extent information to support removing the involved nonviable fascia while retaining the described perfused skin for reassessment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This does not establish that bleeding alone invariably proves tissue viability, and the explanation appropriately requires removal of any additional nonviable tissue found.

The two answer components are balanced across the four choices, and no answer-position cue is counted. Nevertheless, both decisions are heavily scaffolded by the update and the labels; two components do not establish two consequential reasoning steps.

The operative review is temporally clear and stands alone. The current update supplies the findings referenced by the task; it does not require the earlier exploration question. Debridement extent and tissue viability are high-yield surgical objectives.
suggestions: Keep the observed fascial extent, skin perfusion, muscle response and a clear planned reassessment. Move the advance statement that tissue will be retained into post-answer feedback.
Retain enough supported information to establish the viability boundary, but ask the resident to interpret it rather than presenting a categorical viability conclusion followed by its matching plan.

Reassess the proposed competing resection plans with clinical sign-off. A fair moderate item needs a credible extent or tissue-preservation error, not only complete removal versus knowingly leaving described disease. Do not withhold necessary findings or invent viability cutoffs to create difficulty.

title: Persistent axillary drainage — procedure selection
fairness: The supplied findings support a persistent superficial communicating tract despite improvement in new inflammatory nodules. Choosing deroofing requires distinguishing that structural problem from an acute collection and then matching procedural extent to the localized burden. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The established HS diagnosis is appropriate background for this management task and does not identify the procedure by itself. Probe passage is an observed anatomical finding, not a diagnosis-label shortcut. All options name axillary procedures with comparable specificity.

Incision and drainage is less suitable for the described non-distended communicating structure. Regional excision is a real chronic-disease option, but the localized mapped finding and freely mobile surrounding skin favor the offered lesion-directed procedure. This ranking does not imply that every excisional technique is inappropriate for localized HS; limited excision is not one of the offered choices.

The case supplies its own treatment response and procedural mapping. It stands alone without an earlier staging or treatment answer. Matching acute versus chronic structural HS disease to procedural scope is high-yield, with moderate rather than hard discrimination here.

title: Painful cleft swelling — acute drainage access

cues.phrase: An earlier needle aspiration relieved the pressure briefly, but the swelling returned.
cues.why: Paired with 'Repeat needle aspiration of the swelling', the presentation enables an unsuccessful-treatment/repeat-treatment elimination without medical knowledge. It does not identify the final key by itself, but leaves a straightforward lateral-versus-midline access recall question.

fairness: The acute fluctuant lesion, pits and location support pilonidal abscess drainage. Lateral incision and drainage is a defensible intended key among the stated options; no confident clinical error identified.

The exact attribution of a lateral-access recommendation to ESCP has not been independently checked in this offline review. That claim should remain subject to the existing source and clinical-sign-off process, rather than being treated as verified because it appears in the explanation.

Two choices already provide incision and drainage, while the third repeats the documented transient procedure. Recognizing an acute collection therefore supplies little additional scored discrimination; the remaining distinction is access-route recall. This is not a hard two-step resident item.
The presentation and task are clear and self-contained. Acute pilonidal source control is high-yield, although the narrow access detail should not be used as evidence of high reasoning difficulty.
suggestions: Replace the replay of the unsuccessful aspiration with a credible current-stage competitor, and make a supported patient finding genuinely change the procedural decision.

If the exact objective is simply the preferred drainage access, keep the item concise and seek explicit acceptance as a basic technical item. Do not add unrelated complexity or call abscess recognition plus access recall two consequential steps.
Retain the anatomical location and acute findings needed to distinguish the clinical problem; verify the exact route recommendation before clinical approval.

title: Recurrent cleft disease — elective wound strategy
fairness: The candidate explicitly separates resolved acute inflammation from the elective wound decision and states that excision is planned. Off-midline closure is a defensible best choice among the offered wound strategies given recurrence after midline repair and the stated prolonged open-wound care constraint. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The care constraint legitimately favors a closed strategy, but does not distinguish the two closed options without clinical knowledge. It is decision-critical patient context rather than an unfair key-only permission. The prior midline failure is relevant history, not proof that closure in general has failed.

Open secondary healing remains a legitimate alternative in general; the explanation correctly ranks it for this patient's support situation and acknowledges that closure can still require substantial wound care. It does not promise uncomplicated healing.

The two consequential considerations are wound-care feasibility and the relative suitability of closure location in recurrent disease. The competing strategies are specific, parallel and at the same decision stage. This is moderate, high-yield application rather than a guarantee about operative outcomes.
All earlier drainage, operative history and current resolution are restated in the candidate. The elective task stands alone and does not depend on answering the separate acute-drainage item.

title: Low cleft drainage — initial source assessment

cues.phrase: Which assessment should be selected first
cues.why: In an 'initial surgical clinic consultation', the key is the only clinical examination and both distractors are imaging studies. A generic examine-before-scan heuristic can select it without resolving whether the separate pits explain the low opening. This is a decision-stage/category cue, not an absolute rule that examination always precedes imaging.

fairness: A clinical anorectal assessment is a defensible first step for this stable initial consultation. The separate upper pits do not establish the source of a perianal opening. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

MRI and endoanal ultrasonography are real relevant investigations, but both occupy a later or supplementary mapping role in the explanation. The option set mostly compares an initial examination with investigations that could follow it, rather than two closely competing interpretations of the supplied anatomy.
The explanation appropriately acknowledges that examination may not map every fistula and that further imaging can be needed. It does not falsely make an examination a definitive exclusion test.

The candidate is clear and self-contained, with sufficient anatomy and stability information. Avoiding misattribution of low drainage to pilonidal pits is high-yield, but the current option structure does not require that distinction to earn the key.
suggestions: Compare clinically credible assessments at the same stage, or supply actual initial examination findings and test the residual source/mapping decision they create. Do not label findings as proving a fistula or removing uncertainty before the answer.

Use the upper-pit/low-opening relationship to change the scored decision. Apply the deletion test: a generic stable first consultation should not yield the same key merely because it is the only examination.
Keep the exact source uncertain when the observations do not establish it; do not make physical examination or imaging infallible to force a single answer.

title: Painful back lump — change in procedural phase
fairness: The longstanding pore-bearing lesion and the new tense, tender, fluctuant inflammatory episode support acute drainage rather than proceeding with the previously booked complete excision. The diagnosis is not supplied as a label, and the prior elective indication makes excision a real competing plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The consequential reasoning is to interpret the changed state of the longstanding lesion and let that change the procedural phase. Aspiration is a weaker competitor, but it is a specific alternative decompression procedure rather than a generic reassurance or knowingly untreated lesion.

The explanation correctly distinguishes debris on ultrasound from proof of infection. It also presents inflamed-tissue dissection as less favorable, not an absolute prohibition on all excision in every inflamed cyst. This avoids a false binary based on imaging debris.

All three labels are parallel procedures on the same lesion, without a uniquely complete key, explanatory option wording or nonmedical phrase match. The stem supplies the elective plan and new findings directly; no earlier question is needed.

Recognizing when an acute change alters definitive cyst management is a high-yield surgical decision. The familiar pattern and weaker aspiration competitor keep the difficulty moderate rather than hard.
